title: A Clean Slate for Offline Reinforcement Learning

predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The Introduction claims 'average training speedups of 131.5x and 74.8x against OfflineRL-Kit [16] and CORL [17]'. The paper's own Table 2 (Appendix F) yields per-algorithm speedups of only ~6-21x vs OfflineRL-Kit (mean ~14.5x, max 20.8x for CQL) and ~1.3-18.4x vs CORL (mean ~11x, max 18.4x). Figure 5 caps the per-algorithm speedup at 16x. The headline numbers exceed the largest single-algorithm speedup in the paper's own data by roughly an order of magnitude, so they cannot be averages of the tabulated values.

States 'The unification concept traces back to online RL architectures like Rainbow [38] and Muesli [39]' and 'Other dual optimization frameworks [40] cast offline RL methods under a common umbrella'. In the paper's own reference list, [38] is Stable-Baselines3 (Raffin et al.), [39] is Spinning Up (Achiam), and [40] is rejax (Liesen et al.) - none of which are about unification. The correct entries for the identical claims are [25] (Hessel et al., Rainbow), [26] (Hessel et al., Muesli), and [27] (Sikchi et al., Dual RL), which Appendix L.3 cites correctly.

Direct self-contradiction within one paragraph: 'MoBRAC outperforms other model-based methods for all datasets, except for MOPO in maze2d-large-v1' implies 8 wins / 1 non-win out of 9, while 'MoBRAC outperforms the other model-based methods in 6 out of 9 datasets and is tied with MOPO for 3 others' implies 6 wins / 3 ties. Both statements account for all 9 datasets and are mutually exclusive.

States the evaluation runs 'without equalizing the online tuning budgets or computational cost across methods' and that uncontrolled tuning budgets are 'which we continue here for consistency with original papers'. This contradicts the paper's central methodological contribution (Abstract: 'transparent evaluation procedure that explicitly quantifies online tuning budgets'; Section 3.2: a fixed budget of N pre-deployment interactions applied uniformly). As written, the Results section describes perpetuating exactly the unquantified-tuning problem the proposed procedure exists to eliminate.

Caption reads 'Full comparison of TD3-AWR to prior model-based methods across all datasets', but the figure's legend and panels compare TD3-AWR against IQL and ReBRAC, both of which are model-free algorithms, and TD3-AWR is introduced in Section 5.1 as the paper's model-free method. The model-based comparison is Figure 15 (MoBRAC vs COMBO/MOPO/MOReL).

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 3.3 (Distractor Policy Phenomenon) vs Section 3.2 and Appendix D
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 3.3 asserts performance dips 'are common artifacts of statistical fluctuations and sampling noise in bandit evaluation' and 'likely reflect noise rather than fundamental flaws', while Section 3.2 says 'The importance of this is demonstrated by the emergence of distractor policies' and Appendix D systematically shows 'the probability of preferring an unstable policy increases over time' (mean over 100K random policy orderings) with the dip growing as more policies are subsampled. The paper simultaneously dismisses and demonstrates the same systematic effect.

The augmented value target is printed as v_hat_{t+1} = v_{t+1} + alpha_BC * (a_tilde_{t+1} - a_{t+1}) + alpha_H * H(pi). The BC term is a raw difference of action vectors added to a scalar value target - dimensionally invalid for multi-dimensional action spaces and missing the squared norm - and its sign is positive, whereas a behaviour-cloning penalty must reduce the target for actions deviating from the dataset action (ReBRAC/TD3-BC style: v - alpha_BC * ||a_tilde - a||^2). As printed, the unified critic target does not reduce to the BC-regularized objectives it claims to encapsulate.

predicted_errors.error_location: Section 4.2 (Actor Objective) vs Appendix I.2 Eq. (8) and Table 5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Section 4.2 defines the unified actor loss with five terms (beta_q, beta_BC, beta_H, beta_div, beta_dyn), but Appendix I.2 Eq. (8) defines the same loss with only three terms (no beta_div or beta_dyn), and Eq. (7) places the diversity term in the critic loss (as in EDAC), not the actor loss. Additionally, Section 4.2 claims the critic objective includes 'all referenced methods, including CQL despite its complexity', yet Table 5 (Unifloral hyperparameters of prior algorithms) lists no CQL column.

States TD3-AWR 'underperforms or matches [ReBRAC] on others, such as pen-human and kitchen-mixed', but the paper's own Figure 6 reports pen-human-v1: TD3-AWR ~65-70 vs ReBRAC ~40, i.e. TD3-AWR clearly outperforms ReBRAC on pen-human; and Appendix J reports kitchen-mixed-v0: TD3-AWR ~35 vs ReBRAC ~30, again a win, not a match/loss. Both named examples are inverted relative to the paper's own figure values.

Self-contradictory recommendation: warns that 'limiting evaluation to [MuJoCo locomotion and Adroit tasks from the D4RL suite] risks overfitting hyperparameters to these domains', then immediately recommends 'focusing on widely used tasks such as hopper-medium-v2, halfcheetah-medium-expert-v2, walker2d-medium-replay-v2, pen-human-v1, pen-cloned-v1, pen-expert-v1, kitchen-mixed-v0, and maze2d-large-v1 from the canonical D4RL dataset' - i.e., exactly the D4RL MuJoCo/Adroit/kitchen/maze2d tasks it just cautioned against limiting evaluation to. The justification and the recommendation are mutually undermining.

predicted_errors.error_location: Figure 11b (Appendix E) vs Appendix E.2 and Figure 10c
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 11b ('Difference from the CQL implementation', lines of code) reports Unifloral values LARGER than the baselines' (BC: Unifloral 672 vs CORL 544 vs JAX-CORL 201; EDAC: 945 vs 674 vs 230; ReBRAC: 945 vs 658 vs 208), directly contradicting Appendix E.2's claim 'We minimize the number of lines between implementations' and Figure 10c, where Unifloral parent-child diffs are dramatically smaller than CORL's (CQL<-SAC-N: 38 vs 944; EDAC<-SAC-N: 23 vs 63). Either the table's columns are mislabeled/inverted or the minimal-difference claim is falsified by the paper's own data.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 2 (Appendix F), ReBRAC row vs Figure 5
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 2 gives ReBRAC training time as 8.7 min (CORL) vs 6.8 min (Unifloral), a speedup of only ~1.28x, directly contradicting Figure 5's claimed 8x ReBRAC speedup. The 8.7 min value is also an extreme outlier against every other CORL time (range 15.0-180.3 min); ~54-87 min would be required to support the 8x claim. One of the two reported values must be wrong.

The Conclusion claims TD3-AWR and MoBRAC 'integrate the strengths of existing methods to achieve superior performance over a wide range of tasks', but Section 5.1 states the gains are 'inconsistent in complex domains', 'Variances overlap substantially, indicating comparable performance in many cases', and Section 5.2 reports only 6-of-9 wins with ties elsewhere. The universal-superiority framing overstates the hedged, dataset-dependent results reported in the main text.

predicted_errors.error_location: Table 3 (Appendix G), CQL column vs reproduction claim
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Table 3 reports CQL at 3.3 +/- 1.3 on HalfCheetah-Expert, 1.4 +/- 0.3 on Hopper-Expert, and 2.4 +/- 2.4 on Walker2d-Expert - near-random-policy levels - while the section claims these reimplementations are 'matching the performance of prior implementations [17]'. Published CQL results (and CORL reimplementations) on these expert locomotion datasets are in the ~90-110 range. The near-zero expert scores for CQL alone (while IQL/ReBRAC/BC in the same table score ~93-112) are internally anomalous and materially inconsistent with the matching claim.

The walker2d-medium-replay-v2 panel description states 'Y-axis: 40-80' yet lists TD3-AWR at ~85, a value above the stated axis range; the axis therefore cannot render the reported best-arm score. Minor in isolation but part of a broader pattern of imprecise figure reporting in Appendix J.

summary: Exhaustive-mode verification of 'A Clean Slate for Offline Reinforcement Learning' (80 snippets, all verified) under lenient error sensitivity found 15 above-threshold errors, 6 of them high-confidence (>=0.85). The most serious: (1) the Introduction's headline training-speedup claims of 131.5x/74.8x are contradicted by the paper's own Table 2 and Figure 5, which support only ~6-21x; (2) Related Work attributes Rainbow, Muesli, and dual-optimization unification to refs [38]-[40], which in the paper's own bibliography are Stable-Baselines3, Spinning Up, and rejax (the correct entries [25]-[27] are used properly in Appendix L); (3) Section 5.2 contradicts itself within one paragraph on MoBRAC's win count (all-but-one vs 6-of-9-plus-3-ties); (4) Section 3.3 states online tuning budgets were NOT equalized or controlled, directly contradicting the paper's core contribution of a fixed, transparent tuning-budget evaluation procedure; (5) Figure 14's caption calls IQL/ReBRAC 'model-based methods' when they and TD3-AWR are model-free; (6) Section 3.3 dismisses distractor-policy dips as sampling noise while Section 3.2 and Appendix D systematically demonstrate the phenomenon. Additional confirmed issues include an ill-formed BC term in the unified critic target (Eq. 5: un-squared, wrong-signed, dimensionally invalid action-difference added to a scalar), a 5-term vs 3-term contradiction between the main-text and appendix definitions of the unified actor objective (plus a claimed-but-absent CQL column in Table 5), TD3-AWR/ReBRAC examples in Section 5.1 that invert the paper's own figure values, a self-contradictory D4RL dataset recommendation in Section 3.2, a code-diff table (Figure 11b) contradicting the paper's minimal-difference claim, and a ReBRAC training-time entry in Table 2 (8.7 min) inconsistent with its claimed 8x speedup. Under lenient strictness, three further borderline issues are flagged at lower confidence: a Conclusion that overstates 'superior performance over a wide range of tasks' against the hedged Section 5.1/5.2 results, CQL expert-dataset reproduction scores (~2-3) that contradict the section's claim of matching prior implementations, and a walker2d panel whose reported value exceeds its stated y-axis range. Verdict: NEEDS_CORRECTION.
